newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian satirical paper folds, blames press law.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian satirical paper folds, blames press law.

text.p: Jordan's satirical weekly paper Abed Rebbo folded on Saturday, saying it could not afford to publish under Jordan's tough new press laws.

The paper, already facing three court cases after less than a year of operation, said reporting restrictions and stiffer penalties in the amended press law would open the floodgates to endless litigation.

"We could go to court and face fines of 25,000 dinars ($35,000) every week," editor Youssef Ghishan said. The amended law, issued by royal decree last month, raised fines to a minimum of 15,000 dinars from just 1,000 dinars.
It expanded restrictions on articles, pictures and cartoons which the government considered a threat to the royal family, the government, national security, religion, and public morals.
"Satire needs a high ceiling of freedom. When that ceiling is lowered, we can't operate any more," Ghishan told Reuters.
Abed Rebbo, which said it had a circulation of over 20,000, lampooned government ministers and opposition alike, including Jordan's Islamist parliamentarians.

Saturday's farewell front page showed a figure representing Abed Rebbo, wearing traditional Jordanian kuffiyeh head-dress, with a dagger through his neck and his legs shackled by the word "government".
"His blood is upon you for eternity," read the headline.

"Abed Rebbo cannot be a false witness to martial democracy. The past dictatorships were better than that because they didn't slaughter in the name of the country and they didn't rape democracy in the name of democracy," the editorial said.

Ghishan said other weeklies, which are mostly privately funded opposition papers, would be forced to close by an article in the amended law raising their capital requirements 20-fold to to 300,000 dinars.
"Weekly newspapers don't make much profit. No investor will put forward 300,000 dinars," he said.
